newsitem.title: USA: Illinois high court dismisses school funding suit.
newsitem.headline: Illinois high court dismisses school funding suit.

text.p: The Illinois Supreme Court Friday dismissed a constitutional challenge to the state's school funding system.

The dismissal followed previous rejections of the lawsuit by the Illinois Appellate Court in 1994 and by the Cook County Circuit Court in 1992. The lawsuit was filed in 1990 by a group of 75 school districts.

The schools had claimed the current funding system violated the state constitution's mandate to provide equal educational benefits and opportunities because it failed to correct differences in per pupil spending among district. The schools also argued the current school funding system violated the equal protection clause of the constitution.
School officials expressed disappointment in the high court's ruling and said they would now turn their funding reform efforts to the Illinois General Assembly.

"Clearly the court does not believe education is a fundamental right," said Randy Tinder, superintendent of the Carlinville Unit School District 1 and chairman of the Committee for Education Rights, which filed the lawsuit. "That flies in the face of what every parent and every student believes. We must make sure the legislature protects that right."
Bob Haisman, president of the Illinois Education Association, said that is was essential that educators put "fair school funding square in the lap of the General Assembly this spring."

Since 1994, various proposals have been floated to reform the state's system of funding primary and secondary schools, including a constitutional amendment supported earlier this year by Gov. Jim Edgar, that would have required the state to fund at least 50 percent of education costs in exchange for lower local property taxes.
That proposal, however, failed to gain support in the Illinois General Assembly.
A reaction to the state supreme court's decision was not immediately available from the governor.
